tags.description: Concrete oil tanker (originally Old North State/McKittrick) converted into a gambling ship in 1932, run aground during a New Year's storm in 1937. The wreck lies in 1-6 metres of water off Coronado Beach, mostly buried under shifting sand. A historic curiosity rather than a premier dive site — only meaningfully exposed after major winter storms.
tags.name: SS Monte Carlo
tags.qa_notes: Depth corrected from 20m to 6m (2026-06-27) — wreck lies in 1-6m of water, not 20m. RE-AUDITED 2026-08-28: re-pulled en.wikipedia.org and lajollamom.com. tags.seamark:name: Sunken Harbor
tags.qa_notes: RE-AUDITED 2026-08-28: Confirmed via direct re-read of the Wikipedia HMCS Yukon (DDE 263) article, which states the ship was 'sold for use as an artificial reef and sunk as such at Sunken Harbor off San Diego' and 'scuttled ... at Sunken Harbor off Mission Bay in San Diego ... on 15 July 2000' — so 'Sunken Harbor' IS a genuine place name used by a primary source, not a fabrication. However, no source (Wikipedia, lajolla.com, waterhorsecharters.com, sddivesites.com, timesofsandiego.com) treats it as a separately reviewable dive site with its own profile distinct from HMCS Yukon / Wreck Alley — it remains the location name for where Yukon rests. Marine-life list stripped from markdown: no source names specific species for 'Sunken Harbor' itself; see HMCS Yukon and Wreck Alley entries for per-wreck sourced fauna.

tags.description: WWII PC-461-class patrol submarine chaser, sunk September 11, 1945 in collision with USS Laffey in dense fog off San Diego Bay. One crew member lost. Navy demolition teams demolished the wreck in November 1945 and again in 1983, reducing it to a scattered debris field at 27 metres (90 fsw). Notable for early command by L. Ron Hubbard in 1943. Displacement is reported as 295 tons fully loaded (Wikipedia) or 450 tons (NavSource Naval History) — sources conflict and no third source resolves the discrepancy, so both figures are noted rather than one being asserted as fact.

tags.description: Mackenzie-class Royal Canadian Navy destroyer escort (366ft/111m, pennant DDE 263) intentionally sunk at Sunken Harbor off Mission Beach as an artificial reef. The vessel flooded and sank prematurely in rough weather the night before the planned scuttling ceremony, rolling onto her port side. Sources disagree on the exact date: Wikipedia's infobox and dive-industry sources (sddivesites.com, sandiego.org) date the premature sinking to 14 July 2000, while Wikipedia's own article body states she was 'scuttled ... on 15 July 2000' (the originally planned date) — both dates are noted here rather than asserting one as certain. Water depth 30m (100ft); top of wreck at approximately 18m (60ft). At least five divers have died on this wreck — cold, dark, disorienting, with collapsed superstructure. Advanced certification required; wreck penetration requires specialist training.

The previous markdown's list (lingcod, rockfish, cabezon, wolf eels, garibaldi, sheephead, kelp bass, señorita, spiny lobster, sea lions) was unsourced regional padding for this specific wreck and has been replaced with the lajolla.com-sourced species only.

tags.name: Zuñiga Jetty
tags.qa_notes: RE-AUDITED 2026-08-28. CORRECTION: entry_type changed from 'shore' to 'boat'. Two independent sources found this pass — spearfactor.com and a Spearboard.com forum thread — both state there is no shore-based access point at Zuniga Jetty; it sits at the tip of restricted Naval Air Station North Island property, and divers reach it only by boat or kayak (kayakers park near the NAS North Island back gate and paddle out). The prior 'shore' tag and markdown text describing a Coronado Beach shore entry were not supported by any source and have been corrected. Depth (10m/3-9m range) and marine life (sand bass, calico bass, sheephead, halibut, spiny lobster, sea lions) reconfirmed via spearfactor.com and sandiegohistory.org. cadivingnews.com (zuniga-point page) returned an access error on re-fetch this pass and could not be re-verified live, but is retained as a source since its prior citation is well-established and consistent with the newly found sources.
